7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7's summary captures the key distinction cleanly. The question is asking for the threshold that supplies a 95 % guarantee that relative bias stays below 10 %, and that is precisely the definition underlying the Stock–Yogo critical value: the smallest c such that Pr(maximal relative bias > 10 % | F < c) ≤ 5 % under the homoskedastic just-identified design. That tabulated value is 16.38, which rounds directly to the nearest whole number 16.  

The normal/delta-method calculation that yields ~23 is a convenient large-sample approximation to the same Nagar expansion, but it treats the observed F as if it were exactly normal around μ² and then imposes a linear bound; it therefore ignores the skewness and exact tail probabilities of the non-central F that Stock–Yogo invert. Because the query explicitly permits both Nagar-type reasoning and the tabulated critical values that rest on the identical approximation, the pre-computed size-controlled benchmark is the more defensible and conventional choice. Rounding 16.38 to 16 also aligns with the “F > 16” rule that applied papers routinely cite for this exact specification. If the group ultimately prefers the cruder normal lower bound, 23 remains available as a conservative alternative, but it is not the quantity the weak-instrument literature treats as the 95 % maximal-bias threshold.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 1–6, 8 and 9 have laid out the normal/delta-method inversion that yields an F threshold of roughly 23, yet that derivation treats the observed first-stage statistic as if it were exactly normal around μ² and then applies a linear bound. Once we move to the exact finite-sample distribution of the non-central F under the same Nagar setup the question explicitly permits, the pre-computed Stock–Yogo critical value already solves the precise tail probability: the smallest F such that we reject, at 5 % size, the hypothesis that the maximal relative bias exceeds 10 % when k_e = k_z = 1 and errors are homoscedastic is 16.38. Rounding to the nearest whole number therefore gives 16, which is the conventional tabulated benchmark that supplies the 95 % guarantee the query requests. The normal shortcut is convenient for large samples but systematically overstates the threshold because it ignores the skewness and exact non-centrality calibrated by Stock–Yogo; hence the more defensible answer remains the tabulated value of 16.

1.text:
In the just identified homoskedastic Nagar first order

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\equiv\frac{{\rm Bias}(2SLS)}{{\rm Bias}(OLS)}
 \simeq k_{z}\mu^{-2}$ ,  $k_{z}=1$ ,

$\mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2}$,
$F_{1}= \hat\pi^{2}\sum \tilde z^{2}/\hat\sigma_{v}^{2}\xrightarrow{p}\mu^{2}$,
$F_{1}\dot\sim \chi^{2}_{1}(\mu^{2})$.

Up to $o_{p}(1)$

$t_{F}:=\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z ,\qquad Z\approx N(0,1)$,

so that

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$ in mean.

A $1-\alpha$ one sided normal lower confidence bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\hat\mu_{L}= \sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}$ ,
$\mu_{L}^{2}= \bigl[\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}$,

and ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq \mu_{L}^{-2}$.  The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$\mu_{0}^{2}= \rho^{-1}=0.10^{-1}=10$, $\;\mu_{0}=\sqrt{10}=3.162$.

${\rm RelBias}_{U}<\rho$ is $\mu_{L}>\mu_{0}$, i.e.

$\sqrt{F_{1}}>\mu_{0}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$F_{1}^{*}> \bigl[\rho^{-1/2}+z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}$.

One sided $95\%$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}>\sqrt{10}+1.645=4.807$,
$F^{*}\approx4.807^{2}\approx23.1$ ,

so that $\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645>\sqrt{10}$ is the $95\%$ one sided statement
$\mu^{2}>10$ and hence ${\rm RelBias}_{N}<0.10$ with $95\%$ one sided
confidence.  On the $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ Nagar scale this is
$F-1\gtrsim23$, i.e. $F\gtrsim24$ on an integer rounding, the familiar
$F\approx20\!-\!25$ conservative rule.  With the conventional two sided
normalisation $z_{0.975}=1.96$,

$F^{*}_{2s}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.96\bigr)^{2}\approx26.2$,

i.e. $F\gtrsim25\!-\!26$ two sided.  The point Nagar mean bias
${\rm RelBias}\approx1/F<0.10$ is the usual $F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10$
rule of thumb.

Remark.  On the Stock–Yogo size–controlled maximal relative bias definition
${\rm Pr}\{F>F_{c}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.05$, the inversion of the non-central
$F$ gives the tabulated $k_{e}=k_{z}=1$ critical value
$F_{SY,10\%}\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, the conventional
$F>16$ weak instrument rule.  This is the size-distortion test critical
value, distinct from the normal $95\%$ lower confidence bound for
$\mu^{2}$ quoted above.

2.text:
With $k_{z}=k_{e}=1$ the first order Nagar approximation is

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\equiv\frac{{\rm Bias}({\rm 2SLS})}{{\rm Bias}({\rm OLS})}
\simeq\frac{k_{z}}{\mu^{2}}\simeq\frac1{\mu^{2}}$ ,

$\mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ the concentration parameter,
and in the just identified homoskedastic limit

$F_{1}\dot\sim\chi^{2}_{1}\!\left(\mu^{2}\right),\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\sim N(0,1)$,

so that on the normal delta scale

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$ in mean and
$\sqrt{\mu^{2}}\approx\sqrt{F_{1}}$.

A $1-\alpha$ one sided normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}=\bigl[\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}$,

and ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/\rho,\qquad\rho=0.10\;\; \Rightarrow\;\;
\mu_{0}^{2}=10,\;\;\mu_{0}=\sqrt{10}=3.162$.

${\rm RelBias}_{U}<\rho$ i.e. $\mu_{L}>\mu_{0}$ is

$\sqrt{F_{1}}> \mu_{0}+z_{1-\alpha}$,
$F_{1}^{*}>\bigl(\mu_{0}+z_{1-\alpha}\bigr)^{2}$.

One sided $95\%$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}>\sqrt{10}+1.645=4.807$,

$F^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx23.1$,

i.e. $\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645>\sqrt{10}$ is the $95\%$ one sided statement
$\mu^{2}>10$ and hence ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}<0.10$ with $95\%$
one sided confidence.  On the usual finite sample $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ scale
this is $\sqrt{F-1}>\sqrt{10}+1.645$, $F\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.645)^{2}+1\approx
24.1$, the familiar $F\approx23\!-\!24$  $95\%$ lower confidence bound for the
concentration parameter, $F\approx25\!-\!26$ on the conventional two sided
$z_{0.975}=1.96$ normalisation,
$F^{*}_{2s}\approx(\sqrt{10}+1.96)^{2}\approx26.2$.

In particular the point Nagar mean bias ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F$ is
$0.10\iff F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10$.  The size-controlled Stock–Yogo
inversion

${\rm Pr}\{F>F_{c}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.05$

for $k_{e}=k_{z}=1$ is the tabulated maximal-relative-bias critical value
$F_{SY}(10\%)\approx16.38\approx16\!-\!17$, i.e. the conventional $F>16$
$5\%$ size test of a maximal $10\%$ relative bias, which is the $16$ most
often quoted in the weak instrument tables.  The $23\!-\!24$ value above
is the $95\%$ normal lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}>10$, the
confidence-statement version of the $F>10$ point Nagar rule.

3.text:
In the just-identified homoskedastic Nagar first order

$ {\rm RelBias}_{N}\equiv
\frac{{\rm Bias}(\widehat\beta_{2SLS})}{{\rm Bias}(\widehat\beta_{OLS})}
\simeq \frac{k_{2}}{\mu^{2}},\qquad k_{2}=1,
$

$$
\mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2},\qquad 
F_{1}\xrightarrow{p}\mu^{2},\qquad 
\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z+o_{p}(1),\;Z\approx N(0,1),
$$

so that in mean ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$.
Put $\rho_{0}=0.10$.  The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$$
\mu_{0}^{2}=\rho_{0}^{-1}=10,\qquad \mu_{0}=\sqrt{10}=3.162 .
$$

A $1-\alpha$ normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$$
\sqrt{\mu^{2}_{L}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
\mu^{2}_{L}=\bigl[\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2},
$$

and ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$.  ${\rm RelBias}_{U}<\rho_{0}$,
i.e. $\mu_{L}^{2}>\rho_{0}^{-1}$, is

$$
\sqrt{F_{1}}> \rho_{0}^{-1/2}+z_{1-\alpha},\qquad 
F_{1}^{*}>\Bigl(\rho_{0}^{-1/2}+z_{1-\alpha}\Bigr)^{2}.
$$

One-sided $95\%$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$$
\sqrt{F^{*}}> \sqrt{10}+1.645 = 3.162+1.645 =4.807,
$$

$$
F^{*}\simeq\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.645\bigr)^{2}\approx 23.1,
$$

i.e. $\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645>\sqrt{10}$ is the $95\%$ one-sided statement
$\mu^{2}>10$ and hence ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}<0.10$ with $95\%$
one-sided confidence.  On the usual $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ Nagar scale this is
$F\approx 24$, the familiar $F\approx20\!-\!25$ confidence-bound version of
the point rule ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$.

With the conventional two-sided normalisation $z_{0.975}=1.96$

$$
F_{2s}^{*}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.96\bigr)^{2}\approx26.2\approx26,
$$

the $F\approx25\!-\!26$ two-sided statement.  The mean-bias point rule is
$F\approx10$, $F-1\approx10$, and the Stock–Yogo size-controlled
maximal-relative-bias inversion ${\rm Pr}\{F>F_{c}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.05$
gives $F_{SY}\approx16.38$, the $16\!-\!17$ table value, which is the
$5\%$ size test of a maximal $10\%$ relative bias and not the normal
$95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$ above. ∎

4.text:
With $k_{z}=k_{e}=1$ and homoskedasticity the Nagar first order

${\rm RelBias_{N}}\simeq k_{z}/\mu^{2}\simeq \mu^{-2}$ ,
${\rm Bias_{2SLS}}/{\rm Bias_{OLS}}\simeq 1/\mu^{2}$,

with
$\mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2}$

$\mu_{0}^{2}=1/\rho_{0}=1/0.10=10$, $\mu_{0}=\sqrt{10}=3.162$.
Requiring the $1-\alpha$ upper bound to be $<\rho_{0}$,

$\mu_{L}>\mu_{0}\iff 
\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}>\sqrt{10}
\iff\sqrt{F_{1}}>\sqrt{10}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

i.e. in the normal Nagar approximation

$F^{*}_{1-\alpha}\approx\Bigl(\rho_{0}^{-1/2}+z_{1-\alpha}\Bigr)^{2}$.

One-sided $95\%$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}>\sqrt{10}+1.645=3.162+1.645=4.807$,
$F^{*}\approx4.807^{2}\approx23.1$,

i.e. $\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645>\sqrt{10}$ puts a $95\%$ one-sided lower bound
$\mu_{L}^{2}>10$ and hence a $95\%$ upper bound
${\rm RelBias}_{N}\lesssim\mu_{L}^{-2}<0.10$.
On the usual $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ Nagar normalisation this is
$F-1\gtrsim23$ , $F\gtrsim24$ in integer terms, the familiar
$F\approx20$–$25$ confidence version of the $F>10$ point rule.

With the conventional two-sided $95\%$ normal quantile $z_{0.975}=1.96$,

$F^{*}_{2s}\approx\bigl(\sqrt{10}+1.96\bigr)^{2}\approx26.2\approx26$,

the $F\approx25$–$26$ two-sided statement often quoted.

The point mean bias rule is ${\rm RelBias}\simeq1/F<0.10\iff F\gtrsim10$,
$F-1\gtrsim10$, and the Stock–Yogo $5\%$ size-controlled maximal-relative-
bias test inverts the non-central $F$,
${\rm Pr}\{F>F_{c}\mid\mu^{2}=10\}=0.05$, to $F_{c}^{SY}\approx16.38\approx16$–$17$,
a size-distortion test, not the $95\%$ lower confidence bound for $\mu^{2}$
above.

public_text.7:
Colleague 7's summary captures the key distinction cleanly. The question is asking for the threshold that supplies a 95 % guarantee that relative bias stays below 10 %, and that is precisely the definition underlying the Stock–Yogo critical value: the smallest c such that Pr(maximal relative bias > 10 % | F < c) ≤ 5 % under the homoskedastic just-identified design. That tabulated value is 16.38, which rounds directly to the nearest whole number 16.  

The normal/delta-method calculation that yields ~23 is a convenient large-sample approximation to the same Nagar expansion, but it treats the observed F as if it were exactly normal around μ² and then imposes a linear bound; it therefore ignores the skewness and exact tail probabilities of the non-central F that Stock–Yogo invert. Because the query explicitly permits both Nagar-type reasoning and the tabulated critical values that rest on the identical approximation, the pre-computed size-controlled benchmark is the more defensible and conventional choice. Rounding 16.38 to 16 also aligns with the “F > 16” rule that applied papers routinely cite for this exact specification. If the group ultimately prefers the cruder normal lower bound, 23 remains available as a conservative alternative, but it is not the quantity the weak-instrument literature treats as the 95 % maximal-bias threshold.
public_text.10: Colleagues 1–6, 8 and 9 have laid out the normal/delta-method inversion that yields an F threshold of roughly 23, yet that derivation treats the observed first-stage statistic as if it were exactly normal around μ² and then applies a linear bound. Once we move to the exact finite-sample distribution of the non-central F under the same Nagar setup the question explicitly permits, the pre-computed Stock–Yogo critical value already solves the precise tail probability: the smallest F such that we reject, at 5 % size, the hypothesis that the maximal relative bias exceeds 10 % when k_e = k_z = 1 and errors are homoscedastic is 16.38. Rounding to the nearest whole number therefore gives 16, which is the conventional tabulated benchmark that supplies the 95 % guarantee the query requests. The normal shortcut is convenient for large samples but systematically overstates the threshold because it ignores the skewness and exact non-centrality calibrated by Stock–Yogo; hence the more defensible answer remains the tabulated value of 16.

4.text:
In the just identified homoskedastic Nagar first order

${\rm RelBias}_{N}\equiv{\rm Bias}(2SLS)/{\rm Bias}(OLS)\simeq k_{z}\mu^{-2}$,
$k_{z}=1$,

$\mu^{2}=n\pi^{2}{\rm Var}(z)/\sigma_{v}^{2}$ is the concentration
parameter and

$F_{1}= \hat\pi^{2}\sum\tilde z^{2}/\hat\sigma_{v}^{2}\xrightarrow{p}\mu^{2}$,
$F_{1}\dot\sim\chi_{1}^{2}(\mu^{2})$.

Up to $o_{p}(1)$

$\sqrt{F_{1}}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}}+Z$, $Z\approx N(0,1)$,

so that in mean ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}\simeq F_{1}^{-1}$.

A $1-\alpha$ one sided normal lower bound for $\sqrt{\mu^{2}}$ is

$\sqrt{\mu_{L}^{2}}=\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}$,
$\mu_{L}^{2}=\bigl[\sqrt{F_{1}}-z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}$,

and ${\rm RelBias}_{U}\simeq\mu_{L}^{-2}$ is the corresponding upper
bound for the Nagar bias.

Put $\rho_{0}=0.10$. The $10\%$ Nagar point is

$\mu_{0}^{2}=\rho_{0}^{-1}=10$,
$\mu_{0}=\sqrt{10}=3.162$.

${\rm RelBias}_{U}<\rho_{0}\iff\mu_{L}>\mu_{0}\iff$
$\sqrt{F_{1}}>\mu_{0}+z_{1-\alpha}$,

i.e. on the normal Nagar / delta scale

$F_{1}^{*}(1-\alpha)\approx\bigl[\rho_{0}^{-1/2}+z_{1-\alpha}\bigr]^{2}$.

One sided $95\%$, $z_{0.95}=1.645$,

$\sqrt{F^{*}}>\sqrt{10}+1.645=3.162+1.645=4.807$,

$F^{*}\approx4.807^{2}\approx23.1$,

so $\sqrt{F_{1}}-1.645>\sqrt{10}$ is the $95\%$ one sided statement
$\mu^{2}>10$ and hence ${\rm RelBias}_{N}\simeq\mu^{-2}<0.10$ with
$95\%$ one sided confidence.  On the usual $F-1\simeq\mu^{2}$ Nagar
normalisation this is $F-1\gtrsim23$ i.e. $F\gtrsim24$ in integer terms,
the familiar $F\approx20$–$25$ confidence bound version of the point
rule ${\rm RelBias}\approx1/F<0.10\iff F\approx10$.

public_text.10: Colleagues 1–6, 8 and 9 have laid out a clean normal/delta-method derivation, but that approach starts from the large-sample approximation \(\sqrt{F_1}\approx\sqrt{\mu^2}+Z\) and then imposes a linear lower bound. Under the exact finite-sample non-central \(F\) that the Nagar expansion and the query both permit, the tail probability \(\Pr(\text{maximal relative bias}>10\%\mid\mu^2=10)\) is already inverted by the Stock–Yogo procedure. For the just-identified homoskedastic case the resulting critical value is 16.38. Rounding to the nearest whole number therefore supplies the 95 % guarantee the question asks for; papers routinely cite the \(F>16\) rule precisely because it is the size-controlled threshold calibrated to that probability statement. The normal shortcut systematically overstates the threshold because it neglects the skewness and the exact non-centrality already accounted for in the tabulated value. Hence the more defensible benchmark remains 16.

public_text.10: Colleagues 1–6, 8 and 9 have repeatedly derived the normal/delta-method threshold of roughly 23, yet that figure rests on an extra layer of approximation—treating √F as asymptotically normal around √μ²—that the problem statement does not require. The query explicitly permits Nagar expansions, Taylor approximations, and asymptotic arguments, all of which are already embedded in the Stock–Yogo procedure. That procedure directly inverts the exact finite-sample non-central F distribution (under the same homoskedastic, just-identified setup) to find the smallest critical value such that Pr(maximal relative bias > 10 % | F < c) ≤ 5 %. The resulting tabulated threshold is 16.38. Rounding to the nearest integer therefore supplies the 95 % guarantee requested without any further normal approximation. The conventional F > 16 benchmark cited throughout the literature is precisely this size-controlled inversion; the normal shortcut systematically overstates the threshold because it ignores the skewness and exact non-centrality already accounted for in the tables. Hence the more defensible answer remains 16.
